findings.target: internal/postgres/migrate.go + cmd/api/main.go serverChain + the app DSN (R1 work item 4 claims to close this)
findings.finding: R1 adds `lock_timeout` to the MIGRATOR, and the plan treats that as closing the database lens's stall finding. It does not. `lock_timeout` bounds how long the migration waits; it does nothing for the requests that queue behind the migration's pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and nothing for any other lock. Those requests have no bound at all: `serverChain` is documented as `httpx.Base` MINUS `Timeout` (no REQUEST_TIMEOUT in config), the app DSN carries no `statement_timeout` and no `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` (R4 item 8 defers both, conditionally), and `db.Conn()` has no acquire deadline. So a request blocked on a lock hangs indefinitely holding a pool slot, and DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS=8 of them take the whole API down. Throughout, the container reports healthy.
findings.evidence: Executed on an isolated copy of the shipped stack (project tlops, ports 8099/5499) with a synthetic 0002 of exactly R1's shape (two ALTERs + the DEC-82 backfill on `trips`), against a session holding ACCESS SHARE on `trips`. (a) One `GET /v1/logbook` with the ALTER queued: curl http=000 at its own 30s --max-time — no status, no body, no error, nothing. `/healthz` answered 200 in 4.7ms the whole time, because it pings and never touches `trips`. (b) 10 concurrent `GET /v1/logbook`: all ten returned 000 after 18.797-18.801s, releasing only when the lock cleared. `pg_stat_activity` during: 9 backends `active/Lock`, 1 `active/Timeout`. (c) With the pool exhausted `/healthz` flipped to 503 after stalling the full `healthzPingTimeout` of 2.004s — so /healthz's answer is a fact about the pool, not about whether the API can serve. (d) `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}'` said `healthy` through all of it. (e) The real Migrator waited 87.529s for that lock and then succeeded — inside `migrateTimeout` (2m), and no `lock_timeout` in play.
findings.fix: Three separate things, and R1 only does the first. (1) Keep R1's `lock_timeout` on the migration connection. (2) Put `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on cmd/api's DSN in the SAME step, not conditionally in R4 item 8 — a number chosen and written beats a number deferred, and 15s/60s are defensible starting values for one traveller. (3) Wire `httpx.Timeout` with a REQUEST_TIMEOUT variable; `internal/httpx` already has the middleware and main.go already states the only reason it is absent is a missing config variable. Add one leg that holds a lock and asserts the request gets a bounded 503, not silence.

findings.target: internal/postgres/migrate.go `apply()` no-transaction branch; R3 (which writes migration 0003)
findings.finding: A `-- migrate:no-transaction` file that fails part way is an unrecoverable boot loop. The runner applies statements 1..i, writes no `schema_migrations` row, and every subsequent boot re-runs the file from statement 1 — failing on an already-applied statement with a DIFFERENT error that hides the original fault. `restart: unless-stopped` retries this forever. There is no repair flag, no documented manual procedure, and — the sharp part — nothing enforces the re-runnability the runner's own comment demands ("such a file must be written to be re-runnable"): no test, no lint, no acceptance check. R3 is the step that introduces 0003, and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY is precisely the statement class that needs the directive AND that leaves an INVALID index behind on failure.
findings.evidence: Executed against the real Migrator. 0003 with the directive, three statements: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (ok), CREATE TABLE probe_half_applied (ok), SELECT 1/0 (fails). Run 1: `err=postgres: 0003_probe_notx.up.sql statement 3 (no-transaction, so statements 1..2 are already applied): ERROR: division by zero`, exit 1. `SELECT version FROM schema_migrations` -> 0001, 0002 only. Both artefacts present: `table_created=t index_created=t`. Runs 2 and 3, byte-identical file, exactly what a container restart does: `statement 2 ... ERROR: relation "probe_half_applied" already exists`, exit 1, every time. The division by zero — the actual fault — is no longer reachable from any run after the first.
findings.fix: Land the guard with R3, not with the incident. (a) A test that runs every no-transaction migration TWICE against the same database and requires the second run to be clean — that is what 're-runnable' means and it is mechanically checkable. (b) An `IF NOT EXISTS` / `DROP ... IF EXISTS` requirement stated in the file header and greppable. (c) A documented recovery: the exact psql to inspect `schema_migrations`, plus `DROP INDEX ... ` for the INVALID-index case that CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves. (d) Make the failure message carry the version and the statement TEXT, not just the ordinal, so log line one is enough.

findings.target: R4 (`make seed`, work items 3 and 5) against ruling DEC-86
findings.finding: DEC-86 was ruled minutes ago and R4 was written before it; together they lock the owner out of their own deployment with a published credential. R4 item 5: the seed 'creates ONE traveller with a known address and passphrase, printed on completion'. DEC-86: `POST /v1/auth/register` refuses once ANY traveller row exists. R4 item 3's refusal is scoped to 'a non-empty log' — a freshly migrated production database is empty, so the guard does not fire. `make up && make seed` is the obvious first thing an operator types. The result is a deployment whose only account has a passphrase printed in a terminal (and, per DEC-75, checked into a fixture), carrying a 600/min budget, and registration is now closed so the real traveller can never create theirs. The converse is unspecified too: after the real user registers but before they write anything, it is not stated whether 'non-empty log' counts a traveller row.
findings.evidence: Read across three documents that have not been read against each other: plan-v7.json R4 work items 3 and 5; rulings-v3-pending.json DEC-86 consequence ('refuses once any traveller row exists'); DEC-75 consequence ('IT IS A DEV COMMAND AND MUST SAY SO — never run at boot, never in production, and the target refuses against a non-empty log rather than merging'). DEC-75 states the intent correctly and R4 implements a guard that does not deliver it. No code exists to test — internal/seed/load.go is a 25-line stub.
findings.fix: Restate R4's refusal as `refuses when any traveller row exists`, not `when the log is non-empty` — that is one predicate, it covers both directions, and it is the same predicate DEC-86 already puts on register. Keep PD-02's required `-dsn` flag. Add a second guard the plan does not have: refuse unless an explicit `--i-know-this-is-a-dev-database` or an environment marker is present, because the DSN alone cannot tell a dev database from a production one. And do not print a fixed passphrase — generate one per run so the fixture cannot become a shipped credential.

findings.finding: The Dockerfile makes nesting budgets an explicit rule and writes out three of them — ping 2s < probe 3s < timeout 4s < interval 5s. There is a fourth and it does not nest: the server does not begin listening until migrations finish, `migrateTimeout` allows 120s, and the health budget expires at start_period 3s + retries 12 x interval 5s = 63s. A migration that legitimately takes longer than ~63s (a lock wait is the ordinary case) makes the container go unhealthy DURING a correct boot, `make up --wait` reports a failed deploy, and the natural operator response — down, or restart — interrupts a migration mid-flight.
findings.evidence: Executed end to end. Built an image from a copy of the tree with a pending 0005 (`ALTER TABLE trips ADD COLUMN ...`), held ACCESS SHARE on `trips` for 100s, started the container with the shipped HEALTHCHECK parameters. Sampled every 5s: `health=starting` through t=56s (streak 11), `health=unhealthy` at t=61s (streak 12), still unhealthy at t=107s. Container logs: `database ready` at 00:25:39, `migrate: applied version=0005` at 00:27:17, `listening addr=:8080` at 00:27:17 — the migration was correct and in flight for the entire unhealthy window. Separately measured: the 63s figure matches the Postgres-kill run exactly (kill at 00:13:25, unhealthy observed 00:14:24 = 59s).
findings.fix: Raise `start_period` above `migrateTimeout` — `start_period: 150s` costs nothing, because a check that passes during the start period marks the container healthy immediately (the compose file already states this about Postgres). Or split the migration out of boot: `make migrate` already exists and `-migrate-only` already works, so a deploy can run migrations as a separate gated step and boot a server that only ever listens. Say which, in the same comment block that nests the other three.

findings.finding: `unless-stopped` does not restart a container that was stopped from outside, and that decision persists across daemon restart and host reboot — which is the entire difference between it and `always`. So `docker stop travellog-postgres-1` (to look at something, to take a dump, to free memory) followed by a reboot leaves Postgres permanently down on an unattended box, with the API crash-looping beside it and nothing reporting either. Nothing in the repository weighs `always` against `unless-stopped`; the line is in the compose file uncommented, which is unusual for this file.
findings.evidence: Executed as a controlled pair, because the distinction is invisible by inspection. (A) `docker run -d --restart unless-stopped alpine sh -c 'sleep 3; exit 1'` — process dies on its own: after 20s `status=restarting restarts=6`. (B) `docker run -d --restart unless-stopped alpine sh -c 'sleep 3600'` then `docker kill`: after 20s `status=exited restarts=0` — never restarted. Confirmed on the real service first: `docker kill tlops-postgres-1` left it `exited restarts=0 exit=137` and it was still exited 100+ seconds later, while the API sat at `healthy` and every request 500'd.
findings.fix: For an unattended personal VPS, `restart: always` on both services is the right default, and the compose file should say why in the same voice it uses for `pgdata` and the pg_isready flag: `unless-stopped` remembers a human decision that the human will not remember. Keep `unless-stopped` only if the box is one somebody is sitting at.

findings.target: the whole deployment — no backup exists, and `make slice` destroys the volume
findings.finding: Nobody has mentioned backups once, and the tooling actively destroys the only copy. `travellog_pgdata` is the sole copy of a user's log. `scripts/slice-arc.sh:389-390` runs `docker compose down -v` against the DEFAULT project name `travellog` as its first step, with no confirmation and no check on what the volume holds — `make slice` is a plain target. That is correct today (the volume holds nothing) and catastrophic the moment R4's seed or a real traveller has written to it. R2 makes it worse by adding a second stateful volume whose contents cannot be reconstructed from the first, and the two have an ORDERING constraint nobody has stated.
findings.evidence: grep over docs/plan-v7.json: `backup` 0 hits, `pg_dump` 0, `rotat` 0. grep over CLAUDE.md (207 KB): every `restore` hit is about mutation-testing file restores, not data. `scripts/slice-arc.sh` line 389: `step "A0: docker compose down -v — the volume goes, so what follows is real"` followed by `"${COMPOSE[@]}" down -v`, where COMPOSE is `docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml` and the compose file sets `name: travellog`.
findings.fix: Smallest honest answer for one traveller on one box, three lines and no new service: (1) a host cron running `docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -Fc -U travellog travellog > /var/backups/travellog-$(date +\%F).dump`, keep 7, and it is a custom-format dump so `pg_restore` works across a minor version bump; (2) one restore rehearsal, once, recorded in EVIDENCE.md with its output — a backup nobody has restored is not a backup, and this project already holds that standard for everything else; (3) `make slice` refuses when the volume holds a traveller row, or runs under its own project name the way its later phases already do (`COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=$project`, lines 563/636 — the pattern is in the file, just not at A0). When R2 lands: back up the BUCKET first and the DATABASE second. A dump newer than the bucket copy references objects that were never copied; a bucket copy newer than the dump only leaves unreferenced garbage.

findings.target: R2 — MinIO as the third compose service (work item 6), and definition_of_done item 2
findings.finding: Nothing creates the bucket, and neither MinIO's healthcheck nor R2's acceptance check can see that it is missing. `up -d --wait` reports three healthy services against a MinIO that cannot store anything. Because presigning is offline signing, `PresignPut` against a non-existent bucket SUCCEEDS and returns a perfectly-formed URL — the failure surfaces on the phone as `NoSuchBucket` on the PUT. That is precisely the fail-open shape R2 is careful about for the checksum and the length, arriving through a different door. Two further gaps in the same item: R2 pins MinIO for the TEST compose file ('deploy/docker-compose.test.yml (NEW — the PINNED MinIO the integration legs use)') and says nothing about pinning the SHIPPED one — pinned backwards, and the compose file already carries a long comment about why an unpinned Postgres tag would silently orphan a named volume. And nothing states whether `api` gains `depends_on: minio: condition: service_healthy`, nor whether cmd/api reaches the object store at boot the way `run()` pings Postgres — main.go's ping is argued at length as 'a failure here is a real misconfiguration and the process should not come up pretending otherwise', and item 9 of R2 gives media only a nil-check at wiring time.
findings.evidence: Executed against the official image at a pinned tag (`minio/minio:RELEASE.2025-04-22T22-12-26Z`), fresh volume, no init: `curl /minio/health/live` -> 200, `curl /minio/health/ready` -> 200, `ls /data` -> `.minio.sys` only, `ls /data | wc -l` -> 0. The official image auto-creates no bucket (`MINIO_DEFAULT_BUCKETS` is a Bitnami variable, not a MinIO one). grep over plan-v7.json: `MakeBucket` 0 hits, `mc mb` 0 hits, across 41 mentions of `bucket`. Also measured, for the sizing question: MinIO idle RSS is 214.7 MiB — larger than the API (12.4) and Postgres (29.9) combined.
findings.fix: Create the bucket explicitly and prove it. Either a `minio/mc` one-shot service with `depends_on: minio: service_healthy` running `mc mb --ignore-existing`, or `MakeBucket`+`BucketExists` in the media store's constructor at boot (which also gives you the connectivity check main.go gives Postgres). Then make the DoD assert the bucket, not the process: `mc ls` naming it, or a round-trip PUT+GET in the `up --wait` arc. Pin the shipped MinIO tag with the same comment `postgres:17` carries. Add `depends_on: minio: service_healthy` to api.

findings.finding: With Postgres gone, `/healthz` correctly answers 503 and every real route answers `500 {"code":"internal"}` with no `Retry-After`. A 500 tells a client the server has a bug — do not retry, the request is poison — when the truth is 'the dependency is down, retry shortly'. The client this serves is a phone whose whole model is 'a change you can see is a change on disk'; it needs to distinguish 'your write was rejected' from 'try again in a minute'. It is also unanswerable from the logs afterwards: a 500 count conflates handler bugs with database outages.
findings.evidence: Executed. `docker kill` on Postgres, then `GET /v1/logbook`: `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error`, body `{"code":"internal"}`, no Retry-After, repeated over six samples. Same instant, `/healthz` -> 503. Log lines, correctly paired by requestId: `"msg":"auth: the request failed" ... "err":"postgres: looking up a session: failed to connect ... lookup postgres on 127.0.0.11:53: no such host"` then `"msg":"request","status":500`.
findings.fix: Map driver-level connectivity errors (pgconn connect failures, `sql.ErrConnDone`, a pool-acquire deadline) to 503 with `Retry-After: 5`, and leave 500 for genuine handler faults. The error taxonomy in `internal/httpx/errors.go` already exists; this is one code and one branch. Assert it with the same kill-Postgres shape used above.

findings.target: observability — internal/httpx/middleware.go AccessLog, and what R5-R8 must be told to log
findings.finding: The mechanism is good and the fields are thin in ways that get expensive later. (a) `durationMs` is an int64 of milliseconds, so every request under 1ms logs `durationMs:0` — 15,151 of 15,960 lines on the live stack say exactly that, and no latency question is answerable from these logs at all. (b) No traveller id on the access line; with one traveller that costs nothing today and it is the field that has to thread through middleware later. (c) `path` is the raw path, not the route pattern, so once `/v1/trips/{id}` exists nothing aggregates. (d) Nothing mandates that a handler returning an error (as opposed to panicking) logs one ERROR line with the requestId and the driver detail — auth_handlers.go does it, and R5-R8 write fourteen more handlers with no rule stated. A 500 whose only line is the access line is a 3am dead end.
findings.evidence: Live stack, 21.35 hours: 15,960 log lines. `grep -c '"durationMs":0'` covers the overwhelming majority; the only non-zero values observed across the whole sample were `durationMs:4` and `durationMs:9`. Confirmed by reading AccessLog: `slog.Int64("durationMs", time.Since(start).Milliseconds())`. The one ERROR-line pairing that does exist was observed working under the Postgres kill, joined by requestId — which is what shows the shape is right and only the coverage is unstated.
findings.fix: `durationUs` instead of `durationMs` — one word, and it is the difference between having latency data and not. Add `travellerId` to the request-scoped logger where auth already resolves it (the redactor is keyed on substrings of `token`/`passphrase`/`authorization`, so an id is safe). Log the matched pattern alongside the path. And put in the definition of done: every 500 emits exactly one ERROR line carrying requestId and the underlying error, asserted per handler package by a leg that counts lines rather than greps for one.

findings.target: deploy/docker-compose.yml — no `logging:` stanza on either service
findings.finding: No log rotation anywhere, and 95% of what is being kept forever is the healthcheck talking to itself. `LogConfig.Config` is empty on both containers and there are no daemon-level `log-opts`, so the json-file driver runs uncapped.
findings.evidence: Measured on the live stack over 21.35 hours of idle: api log 3,066,153 bytes across 15,960 lines = 143.6 KB/h = 3.4 MB/day = 1.26 GB/year. 15,151 of 15,960 lines (94.9%) are `GET /healthz 200` at the 5s HEALTHCHECK interval. Postgres over 24h: 4,294 bytes, 32 lines. `docker inspect --format '{{json .HostConfig.LogConfig}}'` -> `{"Type":"json-file","Config":{}}`; `~/.docker/daemon.json` has no `log-opts`.
findings.fix: Two one-line fixes and take both. `logging: {driver: json-file, options: {max-size: "10m", max-file: "3"}}` on both services. And do not access-log `/healthz` at Info — either skip the probe's own path in AccessLog or log it at Debug. The disk cost is survivable on any VPS; the signal cost is a 20:1 dilution of the one file you read at 3am.

findings.target: cmd/api/main.go `run()` — the startup ping's error text
findings.finding: The boot failure message names the BUDGET rather than the elapsed time, so a fast failure reads as a slow one. `"the database did not answer within 10s"` is printed for a DNS failure that took 250ms.
findings.evidence: Executed. Started the API alone with Postgres down: `{"level":"ERROR","msg":"api: stopping","err":"the database did not answer within 10s: failed to connect ... hostname resolving error: lookup postgres on 127.0.0.11:53: no such host"}` — nine of them, at 00:16:26.9, :27.1, :27.5, :28.1, :29.0, :30.8, :34.2, :40.7, :53.7. The gaps are Docker's restart backoff, not the ping; each attempt failed in well under a second.
findings.fix: Print the elapsed duration and keep the budget as a second field: `the database did not answer (waited 247ms of a 10s budget)`. One `time.Since(start)`.

findings.target: deploy/docker-compose.yml — no resource limits on any service
findings.finding: `Memory: 0`, `NanoCpus: 0`, `PidsLimit: null` on both containers. On a single-purpose VPS this is defensible; the number that makes it worth a line is the one nobody has: the API's steady working set after Argon2 has run once is an order of magnitude above its idle set, and it does not come back down.
findings.evidence: Measured. `docker stats` on the API container: 12.42 MiB idle. Two concurrent sign-in verifications at ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT=2 (four more were 429'd by the credential limiter, which is the cap and the limiter both working): 140.5 MiB. Still 140.5 MiB a second after the requests completed and after `wait` — Go's scavenger does not return it promptly. So each +1 on ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT is +64 MiB of STEADY working set, not peak. With R2's MinIO measured at 214.7 MiB idle, a 1 GiB VPS is roughly half-spent before any data: ~140 (api) + ~215 (minio) + Postgres at its default 128 MB shared_buffers.
findings.fix: Put those three numbers in docs/BEFORE-A-PUBLIC-DEPLOY.md as the sizing derivation, and add `mem_limit` per service so the kernel OOM-killer's choice is yours rather than 'whichever has the largest RSS' — which, after R2, is MinIO, not the API.

findings.target: the HEALTHCHECK's own failure modes — Dockerfile + deploy/docker-compose.yml
findings.finding: Two things about the probe that are not written down. (a) `/healthz` is a LIVENESS probe answering a READINESS question, and its answer is about the connection pool rather than about whether the API can serve — both inversions were observed in a single run. (b) Nothing consumes `unhealthy`. Compose does not restart on it, there is no watchdog, and no orchestrator is planned, so the healthcheck's only real consumer is `--wait` at deploy time. An unhealthy container keeps taking traffic indefinitely and nothing says so.
findings.evidence: Executed, both inversions in one session. 200 while every `GET /v1/logbook` hung on a table lock (the probe pings, it does not touch `trips`). 503 once the pool was exhausted, after stalling the full 2s ping budget. And across the whole Postgres-kill run the container sat at `Up (healthy)` for 59s while every request 500'd, then `unhealthy` for the remaining minutes with no consequence at all.
findings.fix: Say in the compose file what the probe is for and what it is not — one comment, in the voice the pg_isready block already uses. If restart-on-unhealthy is wanted for an unattended box, that is a `willfarrell/autoheal` sidecar or a systemd timer, and it is a deliberate seventh-service conversation rather than a default.

verified_correct: TWO REPLICAS MIGRATING AT THE SAME INSTANT IS SAFE, executed rather than read. Two processes started the same pending migration simultaneously against one database: B applied it in 6.027s and answered ran=[0004]; A waited on the advisory lock, then found it applied, and answered elapsed=6.031s ran=[] err=<nil>, exit 0. `schema_migrations` holds one row per version, `probe_race` exists exactly once. The pinned-*sql.Conn reasoning in migrate.go's header is correct and load-bearing, and the checked `pg_advisory_unlock` never fired its error branch across ~10 runs.

THE API SURVIVES ITS DATABASE AND RECOVERS ON ITS OWN, with no restart and no lost session. Killed Postgres under a running API, then started it again: /healthz went 200 and /v1/logbook went 200 within one probe interval, the database/sql pool reconnected with no intervention, and the bearer token minted before the outage still authenticated afterwards (sessions are rows, not memory). The process never exited and never needed to.

THE MIGRATION 0002 SHAPE IS CHEAP ONCE IT HAS ITS LOCK. The real Migrator applied R1's shape (two ALTER ... SET DEFAULT plus the DEC-82 backfill UPDATE) in milliseconds of actual work; the 87.5s it took was entirely lock wait. The database lens's 'not a table rewrite, relfilenode unchanged' holds.

GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN BUDGETS NEST AS DOCUMENTED, on the two the compose file names: `shutdownTimeout` 10s inside `stop_grace_period` 15s. Observed a clean `"msg":"shutting down"` on `docker stop` with no truncation. The three healthcheck budgets nest as documented too (2s < 3s < 4s < 5s). It is the fourth budget — the migration's — that does not, and that is a finding above rather than a defect in these.

POOL SIZE AGAINST max_connections IS NOT A RISK HERE. DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS=8 against postgres:17's default max_connections=100 leaves headroom for ~10 API processes plus psql and pg_dump. `config.Load`'s refusal of DB_MAX_IDLE_CONNS > DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS is the right guard for the right reason, and the floors on all five integers each prevent a real misreading rather than being tidiness.

CLOCK AND TIMEZONE HAVE NOTHING TO ADD. `time/tzdata` is blank-imported for the scratch runtime (mutation-proved in CLAUDE.md's M-table), container logs are UTC with a `Z` suffix, every timestamp column is timestamptz, and Go's clock and Postgres's `now()` read the same host clock inside one Docker daemon — there is no skew surface between them. NTP on the eventual VPS is the host's business and is correctly not this project's.

NO METRICS AND NO TRACING IS THE RIGHT ANSWER FOR THIS TARGET, and should be written down as a decision rather than left as an absence. One traveller, one box, one process: a Prometheus scrape and a dashboard would be more moving parts than the thing they watch, and the structured access log already answers every question a single-user deployment can ask — once it logs microseconds. The trigger for revisiting is a second box or a second traveller, not traffic volume.

THE CONTAINER RUNTIME POSTURE IS RIGHT AND I RE-CONFIRMED IT INDEPENDENTLY OF THE SECURITY LENS: stage 2 is scratch, USER is numeric 65532:65532, the health probe is the binary's own flag with no shell to invoke, and both published ports are loopback-bound. Building and running the image from a clean copy of the tree reproduced all of it.
questions_for_human: `restart: always` or `restart: unless-stopped`? They differ only after a reboot, and only for a container a human stopped — which is exactly the case an unattended VPS cannot recover from. I would take `always`; the compose file has never argued it either way.

Where should backups land, and who runs them? A host cron writing `pg_dump -Fc` beside the volume is the smallest thing that works and puts nothing new in the stack; a backup container is tidier and is a seventh dependency conversation. Related and separate: should `make slice` refuse to `down -v` a volume that holds a traveller, or should it simply always run under its own project name (the pattern is already in the file at lines 563 and 636)?

Given DEC-86, should `make seed`'s refusal be 'any traveller row exists' rather than 'the log is non-empty'? And should the seeded passphrase be generated per run rather than fixed? The fixed one is currently the only thing standing between `make up && make seed` on a fresh VPS and a locked-out owner.

What number for REQUEST_TIMEOUT, and for `statement_timeout` / `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on cmd/api's DSN? R4 item 8 makes the latter two conditional on 'DEF-03's numbers' being settled, which means they may not land at all. 15s / 15s / 60s are defensible for one traveller and a chosen number beats a deferred one.

Who creates the MinIO bucket — an `mc` one-shot service, or the media store at boot? The second gives you a connectivity check at boot for free, which is what main.go already does for Postgres and what R2 currently gives media only as a nil-check.
Does `docs/BEFORE-A-PUBLIC-DEPLOY.md` need to move earlier than R8? R2 introduces the first real secrets and the second stateful volume, and the checklist lands six steps later.
unverifiable: Everything about MinIO in the running system: R2 has no code. I verified the two claims that are testable against the image itself — zero buckets, health 200/200, no auto-creation, 214.7 MiB idle — but the presigner, the address seam (S3_INTERNAL_ENDPOINT vs S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL), and whether `make up` gates api on minio are all read from plan-v7 rather than run.

`make seed` (R4): internal/seed/load.go is a 25-line stub and cmd/seed does not exist. The half-fail question — whether a failed S3 upload can leave rows without objects or objects without rows — cannot be answered against code, only against R4's text, which puts the ten-table insert in one transaction (correct) and the two PNG uploads outside it (unstated).

Disk exhaustion. I did not fill a disk: the only volume available belongs to the user's live stack, and a scratch-volume fill on Docker Desktop for Mac exercises the VM's disk rather than a VPS's. The log-growth rate above is measured; what Postgres does at 100% is not, and it is the one failure mode where 'the app keeps a green healthcheck' would be worst.

Behaviour behind Caddy, and TLS. Deferred with the third service, so there is no proxy hop, no X-Forwarded-For, and no certificate lifecycle to exercise. The security lens says the same about the rate limiter; the same gap covers TLS termination, certificate renewal failure, and HSTS — none of which exist to break yet.

Whether `restart: unless-stopped`'s stickiness survives a real host reboot, as opposed to a daemon restart. I demonstrated the mechanism (docker kill leaves RestartCount=0 permanently, a self-exit restarts) but did not reboot the user's machine to prove the reboot half; that half is Docker's documented semantics rather than my measurement.

The 63s health budget and the 120s migrate budget were measured against a lock wait I created. I did not measure how long a real 0003 takes on a seeded 284-row database — at that size it will be milliseconds, so the collision is a lock-contention risk rather than a data-volume one. It becomes a data-volume risk at whatever size next_slice's 50,000-photograph generator produces, and nobody has measured that either.
